CalendarConnectIn.description:
A provider and the secret address to connect.

The `address` is the secret ICS/webcal address. It is **write-only**: it goes in
and it is never handed back, in whole or in part, in any response.
CalendarConnectIn.title: CalendarConnectIn

CalendarConnectionOut.description:
One calendar connection, as it is shown to the user.

There is no `address` field and no `fingerprint` field. The fingerprint is a keyed
HMAC and so is not a secret, but it is not the user's business either, and a digest
in a response body is one more thing to leak in a screenshot.

`last_error_kind` is a **slug** (`revoked`, `transient`, …), never a message and
never a URL: an `httpx` exception message contains the full request URL, which *is*
the credential (AD-13).
CalendarConnectionOut.title: CalendarConnectionOut

CalendarReconnectIn.description:
A new address for a connection the provider revoked.

The provider revoked the old secret, so the address the user pastes now is a *new*
one. The connection's row is reused rather than a second row being created.
CalendarReconnectIn.title: CalendarReconnectIn

ConflictOut.description:
One conflict the user must answer.

`actions` is the closed set of three choices for this conflict's kind. `dismiss` is not
among them and cannot be expressed.
ConflictOut.title: ConflictOut

ConflictResolutionIn.description:
The body of a resolution: which of the three, and which event is the new one.

`new_side_id` is required because the pair row is **symmetric** — it stores both sides
sorted, so the row cannot say which side the user just created. The prompt's asymmetry
lives in the client (it knows which event it just made) and comes back here.

The body carries the id only, not the kind: this endpoint resolves conflicts *on
personal events*, so the new side is a personal event by definition. That keeps the
shape narrow — a client cannot name a saved event's id and have it deleted.
ConflictResolutionIn.title: ConflictResolutionIn

ConflictResolutionOut.description:
The outcome of a resolution.

`new_side_id` is the event the prompt called "new" — the client opens it in edit mode
for `edit_new`, or finds it already deleted for `delete_new`.
ConflictResolutionOut.title: ConflictResolutionOut

ConflictSideOut.description:
One side of a conflict: the event that clashes.

The times are UTC instants. The side does not carry a timezone of its own — the sides
are two records that may live in two different zones, and a conflict is about the
instants they occupy, not about how either is displayed.
ConflictSideOut.title: ConflictSideOut

CsrfTokenOut.description:
The CSRF token the frontend sends back on every unsafe request.

The token is also set as the `csrftoken` cookie on the same response; the frontend
reads the cookie and echoes the value in the `X-CSRFToken` header. Sending both is
Django's own convention, and it is the one `CsrfViewMiddleware` checks.
CsrfTokenOut.title: CsrfTokenOut

CurrentUserOut.description:
The signed-in user.

The id and the email are what the frontend needs. There is no password field, no
permission field and no catch-all, so nothing internal can ride along.

The **onboarding status** is here, and it is here because the frontend needs it to
decide between the onboarding flow and the home. It says only whether the onboarding
is finished and which step the user is on — it carries no interests and no digest
preference, because `me` is about *who* the user is and a settings blob there would
grow without bound. The full state lives at `/api/personal/onboarding`.

It is read through `personalization`'s **published interface** — the service, never
the model — because `identity` may not reach into another app's tables (AD-2). The
import contract `models-personalization` proves it.
CurrentUserOut.title: CurrentUserOut

DigestCardOut.description:
One Pulse Card on the digest (FR-6).

**The bucket, not the score.** FR-22's raw `relevance_score` is an internal number;
the card shows 1-5 dots. Sending the score would invite the frontend to re-bucket it
— which is the "recomputed at render" failure wearing a different hat, and would break
the no-flicker rule, since the bucket the user saw this morning is a **persisted fact
about their day**. The Detail Screen's own read carries the score; the card's
contract is the card's.

**The tags are the persisted keys, in the persisted order.** They are not recomputed
and not re-sorted — the order is the priority order, and it is what the card and the
Detail Screen must agree on (AD-10). The client owns the labels.

**The times are instants plus the IANA zone.** AD-6: "display-time conversion happens
at the presentation edge, never in domain logic". The API does not send a
pre-formatted local string.

**The display facts are optional.** They live in the catalog (for a public event) or
in the user's own agenda (for a personal one), and either place may have moved on
since the composition. When they have, `catalog_event_missing` says so and the
*explanation* is still there — the composition is a fact about the day, and its
explanation must not change because a source moved.

**`source_badge` is the variant key, or `None`.** A personal event has no source, so
it has no badge; `None` here means "there is no source", not "unknown". The client
owns the label and the glyph.
DigestCardOut.title: DigestCardOut

DigestOut.description:
The signed-in user's Pulse Digest for their local day (FR-5, FR-8, FR-6).

**`status` says which of the three states this is**, and all three answer **200**.
A 404 would mean "there is no such digest", which is true of `not_composed` and false
of `empty` — and the client would have to map a status code onto "nothing happening"
versus "not ready", which is exactly the interpretation the API is supposed to
remove.

**The city carries its `city_source`,** because the fallback city is not the user's
city: FR-8's copy is "No qualifying events in **{city}**", and if the city is the
server's fallback rather than the user's, the copy is misleading.

**`timezone` is on the response.** The digest row stores the zone it was composed in,
and the client needs it to render the local date it was given. Without it, a client
showing "Wednesday" has no way to know which Wednesday.
DigestOut.title: DigestOut

DigestPreferenceIn.description:
The digest delivery time and timezone, and the two content preferences.

The delivery time is a **local wall clock** — "09:00" means nine in the morning where
the user is, not nine in the morning UTC. The zone says where that is.

**The two new fields are optional, and omission means "leave it alone".** The city
and the opt-out are separate settings, and a client that only wants to change the
delivery time must not silently clear the city or silently re-include personal
events.

**`city` is the user's home city, in the catalog's spelling.** A city the catalog
does not cover is stored as the fallback with `city_source` `fallback`, so the digest
can say "we don't have your city yet" rather than passing the fallback off as the
user's city.

**A `null` city is not a clearing, and this endpoint cannot clear.** A `null` and an
omitted field are the same value here, so "leave it alone" and "clear it" cannot be
told apart — and a shape that cannot say which one it means must not guess. Guessing
"clear" would wipe the city of every client that sends the field as `null`, and
guessing "leave alone" would make the value unreachable. So a `null` city is
**left alone**, and clearing is not offered here at all: the service can clear the
city (`set_home_city(city=None)`), and a future settings endpoint may expose it
through a shape that *can* distinguish the two. Until then, "no city" is reached by
the sign-up path or by the backfill, not by this request.
DigestPreferenceIn.title: DigestPreferenceIn

DigestPreferenceOut.description:
The stored digest delivery time and timezone, and the two content preferences.

`city_source` says how the city was arrived at — `geo`, `choice`, `fallback` or
`backfill`. A client can show "we don't have your city yet" for a fallback rather
than implying New York City is the user's city.
DigestPreferenceOut.title: DigestPreferenceOut

EventListOut.description: One page of the public catalog, and what the frontend needs to page through it.
EventListOut.title: EventListOut

EventOut.description:
One public event.

`id` is the stable identifier the API is keyed by; `slug` is the public page route's
key (the spine's Ids convention: a page URL uses the slug, never the PK).
EventOut.title: EventOut

EventPage.description:
The list endpoint's query parameters.

`city` matches the venue's city exactly, case-insensitively. The date bounds are
inclusive and apply to the start time.
EventPage.title: EventPage

HealthUnavailableOut.description: The shared error shape, with the per-component details typed for the client.
HealthUnavailableOut.title: HealthUnavailableOut

InterestChipOut.description:
One interest chip: its stable key and its display label.

The **key** is what the API accepts and what is stored; the **label** is what the UI
shows. They are separate because a renamed label must not invalidate a stored pick.
InterestChipOut.title: InterestChipOut

InterestChipsOut.description: The ten interest chips, in the order the flow shows them.
InterestChipsOut.title: InterestChipsOut

InterestsIn.description:
The user's interest picks.

The list **replaces** the user's set: it is the whole set, not a delta. An empty list
is valid — that is how the step is skipped, and it clears the set.

The keys are what is sent, never the labels: a label may be renamed, a key may not.
InterestsIn.title: InterestsIn

OnboardingStateOut.description:
The whole onboarding state: the progress, the interests and the digest preference.

The interests and the digest preference are the **stored** values, so a skipped step
shows what the skip wrote (an empty set, the default preference) rather than nothing.
OnboardingStateOut.title: OnboardingStateOut

OnboardingStatusOut.description:
How far through the onboarding the user is.

This is what `GET /api/auth/me` carries. It says **only** whether the onboarding is
finished and which step the user is on — enough for the frontend to choose between the
onboarding flow and the home. It carries no interests and no digest preference: `me`
is about *who* the user is, and a settings blob there would grow without bound.
OnboardingStatusOut.title: OnboardingStatusOut

PasswordResetConfirmIn.description: The reset confirmation: the token from the reset link, and the new password.
PasswordResetConfirmIn.title: PasswordResetConfirmIn

PasswordResetConfirmOut.description:
The reset-confirmation answer.

The password has been changed and the account's other sessions have ended.
PasswordResetConfirmOut.title: PasswordResetConfirmOut

PasswordResetRequestIn.description: The reset request: the address to reset.
PasswordResetRequestIn.title: PasswordResetRequestIn

PasswordResetRequestOut.description:
The reset-request answer. The same for a known address and an unknown one.

It says the request was received, and nothing about whether there is an account.
PasswordResetRequestOut.title: PasswordResetRequestOut

PersonalEventCreateIn.description:
The body of a create.

The IANA timezone is **required**: a floating local time is refused rather than guessed,
because the user's wall clock and the event's zone are not the same thing.
PersonalEventCreateIn.title: PersonalEventCreateIn

PersonalEventListOut.description: The user's own personal events, soonest first.
PersonalEventListOut.title: PersonalEventListOut

PersonalEventListQuery.description:
The query parameters of the list endpoint.

This is a **separate** schema from `PersonalEventListOut`, and it has to be. A
schema-typed argument is a request *body* unless it is wrapped in `Query(...)`; and the
response schema has no bounds on it, so using it as the query model would silently
accept `?starts_after=…` and then ignore it.

The bounds are inclusive and apply to the start time. Both are optional: with neither,
the list is every event the user has.
PersonalEventListQuery.title: PersonalEventListQuery

PersonalEventOut.description:
One personal event.

`version` rises by one on every edit (AD-7's send key uses it, so it may only go up).

`calendar_connection_id` says where the event came from: a connection's id for a row a
calendar imported, `None` for one the user entered. It is the **id** and nothing else
— the secret address never appears in any response shape (AD-18), and this field does
not change that. Onboarding step 1 needs it to show what a calendar just brought in,
and Settings → Sources will need it to say what a connection owns before it is
disconnected.
PersonalEventOut.title: PersonalEventOut

PersonalEventPatchIn.description:
The body of an edit. Every field is optional — an edit changes only what it names.

A field left out is unchanged. There is no way to *clear* `location` or `notes` through
this shape, because `None` and "not mentioned" are the same value here; that is a
deliberate limitation of a first-cut edit endpoint, not an oversight.
PersonalEventPatchIn.title: PersonalEventPatchIn

PreviewCardOut.description: One card in the Pulse Preview.
PreviewCardOut.title: PreviewCardOut

PreviewCitiesOut.description: The supported cities, for the one-tap city picker.
PreviewCitiesOut.title: PreviewCitiesOut

PreviewOut.description:
The preview for a city.

**`city` is always present**, even when `items` is empty: the empty case is a city
the catalog does not cover, and the frontend shows "No preview available in {city}
yet." — it needs the name to say it. It is never another city's name: an
unsupported explicit city returns an empty preview carrying **that** city's name.
PreviewOut.title: PreviewOut

SavedEventListOut.description:
The user's saved events, and how many were left out.

`omitted` counts the saves whose catalog event has since disappeared — superseded or
unpublished. They are not listed, because they have no title to show, but they are not
hidden either: the count lets the client tell the user that something they saved is no
longer available, rather than silently dropping it.
SavedEventListOut.title: SavedEventListOut

SavedEventListQuery.description:
The query parameters of the saved-events list endpoint.

The bounds are inclusive and apply to the **snapshot's** start time — the same value the
list returns — so a filtered item and its own timestamp never disagree (AD-21).
SavedEventListQuery.title: SavedEventListQuery

SavedEventOut.description:
One saved public event.

**The times come from the snapshot; the display fields come from the catalog.** They
are two different places, and keeping them straight is the point (AD-21):

- `start_time_utc` and `end_time_utc` are the **snapshot** — what the user saw when
  they saved, updated only by AD-17 propagation.
- `title`, `venue_name` and `canonical_url` are the **catalog's current** values, read
  at request time. An editorial correction shows up immediately.

`event_version` is the snapshot's version of the catalog event. It is what lets the
system detect that the snapshot is behind, and it is what `stale` is measured against.
SavedEventOut.title: SavedEventOut

SchedulingConflictDetails.description: The `details` of a 409: which event was written, and what it clashes with.
SchedulingConflictDetails.title: SchedulingConflictDetails

SchedulingConflictOut.description:
The 409 a conflicting create or edit answers with.

It is an `ErrorOut` — `{code, message, details?}` — with the `details` field
**narrowed** to the conflict payload. That narrowing is the point: the client has to
render the three actions (FR-58), so the shape of the conflict has to be in the
generated contract, not just in the prose of the description. With the plain `ErrorOut`
the `details` would be an untyped dictionary, and a client generated from the OpenAPI
document could not read a single field of it.

The message and code come from `domain.errors.SchedulingConflictError`; the API layer
builds the body, so the two stay in step through this schema.
SchedulingConflictOut.title: SchedulingConflictOut

SignInIn.description: The sign-in request: an address and a password.
SignInIn.title: SignInIn

SignInOut.description:
The sign-in answer. The same for a wrong password and an unknown address.

The status is the only field. A body that named the account, or said which half of
the pair was wrong, would be the enumeration leak the services are careful to avoid.
SignInOut.title: SignInOut

SignOutOut.description: The sign-out answer. The session is over; nothing else is said.
SignOutOut.title: SignOutOut

SignUpIn.description:
The sign-up request: an address, a password, and optionally a home city.

The password is a plain string here and is never echoed back. It goes to
`apps.identity.services.sign_up`, which validates it against Django's configured
password validators and hashes it.

**`city` is optional, and it is the visitor's preview choice carried across
sign-up.** The preview choice lives in a **session cookie** read in the browser
only — deliberately, because a server-side choice would make `/preview` vary per
visitor and break AD-12's cacheability. So the carry is a **request field**: the
frontend reads the cookie and sends the city here.

A city the catalog does not cover is stored as the fallback with `city_source`
`fallback`, so the digest can say "we don't have your city yet" rather than passing
the fallback off as the user's city. The sign-up **response** says nothing about
it either way — a city is not an account-existence oracle, but the response shape
carries nothing beyond `status` in any case.
SignUpIn.title: SignUpIn

SignUpOut.description:
The sign-up answer. The same for a new address and an existing one.

There is no `created` flag, and no account id: either would say whether the address
was taken. The account holder of an existing address is told by email instead.
SignUpOut.title: SignUpOut

get.description: The CSRF token the frontend sends back on every state-changing request, in the `X-CSRFToken` header. The token is also set as the `csrftoken` cookie on this response, so the frontend can read it from there. This is a safe request, so it is not itself checked for a token.

The signed-in user's id, email and onboarding status. An anonymous request is refused with 401. Nothing internal is returned: there is no password hash, no permission list and no catch-all field. The onboarding status says only whether the onboarding is finished and which step the user is on; the full state is at `/api/personal/onboarding`.

post.description: Asks for a reset link. A known address gets one, by transactional email; an unknown address gets nothing. The answer is the same either way, so the endpoint cannot be used to find out who has an account.

Consumes a reset token and sets a new password. The token is single-use and short-lived: a token that was already used, revoked or expired is refused, and the refusal does not say which of the three it was. The account's other sessions end, so a stolen session does not survive the password change.

Authenticates an email and a password and establishes the session. A wrong password and an unknown address are answered identically — the same status and the same body — so neither can be used to find out who has an account.
Ends the session the request carries. The session cookie is cleared, so the next request is anonymous.

Creates an account. The answer is the same whether the address was new or already taken: an existing account holder is told by email instead. This endpoint does not sign anyone in — call `/api/auth/signin` for that — so the response is byte-identical and header-identical whichever case it was.

`city` is optional: the visitor's home city, carried across from the preview choice. A city the catalog does not cover is stored as the fallback, and the response says nothing about it either way.

get.description: Published, non-superseded events that have not started yet, soonest first. Optional city and date-range filters. No session is used and none is set.
One published event by id. An event that is not public — or that has already started — reads as not found, the same set the list shows. No session is used and none is set.

The user's own calendar connections: the provider, the status, when it last synced and whether a sync is running. The calendar address is **never** returned — it is the credential, and it is write-only. No one else's connections are listed.
get.summary: List the signed-in user's calendar connections

post.description: Connects a calendar by its secret ICS/webcal address. The address is stored encrypted and is never returned. The first sync is **enqueued, not run inline** — the response comes back immediately with the connection's status, and the import lands a moment later. A Free account may hold one calendar; a second connection is refused with a calm upgrade prompt.

delete.description: Disconnects one of the user's calendars. The credential is destroyed and the events that calendar imported are purged, along with their conflict pairs and their reminder plans. The user's own events are untouched.

get.description: One of the user's own calendar connections and its sync state, so onboarding step 1 can show the imported events without leaving the flow. A connection that belongs to somebody else reads as not found.
get.summary: Get one of the signed-in user's calendar connections

post.description: Replaces a revoked calendar's address and brings it back to life. The events it already imported are kept — the provider revoked the address, not the events. A connection that is already active is refused: there is nothing to reconnect, and silently replacing a working credential would change which calendar the user is looking at without them asking.
post.summary: Reconnect a calendar whose access was revoked

get.description:
The user's Pulse Digest for their local day, as it was composed.

The response always says which state it is in: `composed` (there is a digest and it has cards), `empty` (there is a digest and it has none — nothing qualifying near you today), or `not_composed` (the digest has not been built yet). The last two are different facts and the client shows different things for them.

Each card carries the event's name, time and place, up to three Why-this Tag keys, the Confidence Pulse bucket (1-5) and the Source Badge variant. The bucket is sent rather than the raw score: the bucket the user saw this morning is a persisted fact about their day, and a client that re-bucketed it could flicker.

The times are instants plus an IANA timezone; converting them for display is the client's job. `catalog_event_missing` marks a card whose event the catalog no longer holds — the explanation is still there, because a composition is a fact about the day.
get.summary: The signed-in user's Pulse Digest for today

get.description: The user's own personal events, soonest first. No one else's are listed.
get.summary: List the signed-in user's personal events

post.description: Creates a personal event. The IANA timezone is required — a floating local time is refused rather than guessed. If the new event clashes with one already on the calendar, the response is 409 carrying the conflict and the three actions; the client then posts one of them to the resolve endpoint.

Records the user's choice on a conflict prompt. Exactly one of the three actions the prompt offered is accepted; there is no dismiss. A resolution that is illegal for this conflict's kind is refused, and the prompt stays open.

delete.description: Removes one of the signed-in user's personal events.

get.description: One of the signed-in user's personal events. An event that is not theirs reads as not found.

patch.description: Edits a personal event and re-runs conflict detection. A conflicting edit returns the same 409 payload a conflicting create does.

get.description: Where the user is in the 3-step onboarding flow, their interest picks and their digest delivery preference. A user who left mid-step is resumed at the same step within 7 days; after that the flow restarts at step 1. A user who has finished onboarding is never sent back into it.

put.description:
Sets when and where the Pulse Digest should arrive. The delivery time is a local wall clock, so it means nine in the morning where the user is. The timezone must be an IANA zone name.

`city` is the user's home city, in the catalog's own spelling. A city the catalog does not cover is stored as the fallback and reported back with `city_source` set to `fallback`, so the client can say "we don't have your city yet" rather than implying it is the user's city.

`include_personal_events` defaults to included — personal events are in the digest unless the user opts out. Both fields are optional, and **leaving one out does not change it**: an omitted field (and a `null` city) means "leave it alone", so a client that only wants to change the delivery time does not reset the city. This endpoint cannot clear the city — a `null` and an omitted field are the same value, and a shape that cannot tell them apart must not guess.
put.summary: Set the digest delivery time, timezone, home city and personal-events opt-out

get.description: The ten interest chips, in the order the flow shows them. This list comes from the server, so the frontend holds no second copy of it. Each chip carries a stable `key` and a display `label` — send the key back, not the label.

put.description: Replaces the user's interest picks with the given set. At most 3 chips may be picked, and every key must be one the chips endpoint offers. An empty list is valid — that is how the step is skipped, and it clears the set.

post.description: Skips every step and finishes the onboarding. A user who skips everything has still finished onboarding — the default digest preference is written, so the digest has a delivery time to work with.
Moves the user to the next step. Advancing past the last step finishes the onboarding — there is no fourth step. A user who has already finished is not moved again.
post.summary: Advance to the next onboarding step

post.description: Skips the current step. No step requires any input, so every one of them can be skipped. Skipping the interests step clears the picks; skipping the digest step writes the default delivery preference. Skipping the last step finishes the onboarding.

get.description: The user's own saved events, soonest first. The times are the snapshots — what the user saw when they saved — and the titles and venues are the catalog's current values. `omitted` counts the saves whose catalog event has since disappeared; they are not listed, but they are not hidden either.
get.summary: List the signed-in user's saved events

delete.description: Removes one of the signed-in user's saves. The conflict pairs it took part in close as `cleared_by_state_change` — the pair ended because a side went away, which is not a user resolution.

post.description: Saves a public catalog event onto the signed-in user's own calendar. The save is idempotent: saving an event that is already saved returns the existing record. The times in the response are the snapshot taken at save time; `stale` says whether the catalog has moved past it, in which case re-propagation has been requested. If the save clashes with a personal event, the response is 409 carrying the conflict and the three actions.

get.description: Up to three Pulse Cards for a city, each with its Event Fit score and Why-this tags and its Source Badge. With no `city` parameter the city is inferred from the edge's geo header; an explicit `city` overrides it; `use_geo=false` is the visitor's 'Don't use my location' choice and the location is then not consulted at all. The response says which city was resolved and how it was resolved. No session is used and none is set.
get.summary: The Pulse Preview for a city

get.description: The supported cities, alphabetically, for the one-tap city picker. A city is supported when the catalog has at least one upcoming public event with an Event Fit for it. No session is used and none is set.
get.summary: The cities the Pulse Preview can serve
